explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD says they sell "…the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals." I think a pair of sandals is a small price, and that makes the charge sting even more.

A woolen cloak is a fair guess, baker, but verse 6 says something else. The LORD says they sell "…the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals." Garments taken in pledge show up a couple of verses later (Amos 2:8), but that's a separate line.

A belt is a fun guess, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says they sell "…the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals." I think the sandals make the charge sting even more, because it's such a small price.
Yes, baker. The LORD says a man and his father have relations with the same girl "…and so profane My holy name." That's heavy, so I'll just say it plainly. The LORD says it touches His holy name.

This one is true, friend. The LORD says a man and his father have relations with the same girl "…and so profane My holy name." It's a heavy part of the passage, and I think we should treat it that way. The text doesn't water it down, so neither will I.
That's right, baker. The LORD says that in the house of their God, they drink "…wine obtained through fines." It's one of the charges He brings against Israel, and I think it's a heavy one.
Offerings sound like they'd fit the house of God, I'll give you that. But the verse says they drink "…wine obtained through fines." Fines is the word the LORD uses, friend.
Trade sounds so friendly, doesn't it? That's not the word in the verse, though. The LORD says they drink "…wine obtained through fines." The word is fines, friend.

Not quite, baker. The LORD says, "…it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them…" The Amorite was tall like cedars and strong as oaks, so Israel's men weren't the secret ingredient here. The LORD was.

Right, baker. The LORD says, "…it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them…" and the Amorite was "…like that of the cedars…" Israel didn't win by being bigger. He did it, from the fruit above to the roots below.
Yes, Egypt. The LORD says, "…I brought you up from the land of Egypt…" He's reminding Israel of what He did for them. That's quite a list of reminders, and it's only getting started.

Babylon is a sneaky guess, but verse 10 names a different land. The LORD says, "…I brought you up from the land of Egypt…" He's pointing back to what He did for Israel there, and then to the forty years He led them in the wilderness.
Assyria's a good guess, friend, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says, "…I brought you up from the land of Egypt…" He's pointing to where they started, not to a place on a later map.

Forty is right. The LORD says He "…led you forty years in the wilderness…" He led them the whole way, and the goal was that they might take possession of the land of the Amorite. Forty years is a long road, baker.

Seventy is a fair guess, baker, but it's not the number here. The LORD says He "…led you forty years in the wilderness…" It's forty, and He was the one leading, so that they might take possession of the land of the Amorite.
Twelve is a good Bible number, I'll give you that. Not this time, though. The LORD says He "…led you forty years in the wilderness…" Forty years of Him leading the way.
Not this time, baker. The LORD says Israel "…commanded the prophets not to prophesy." These are the prophets He raised up from their own sons (Amos 2:11), and Israel told them not to prophesy.

That's right. The LORD says, "…you made the Nazirites drink wine and commanded the prophets not to prophesy." The prophets were the ones He raised up, and Israel told them to stop. They told them to hush.
Yes, their escape, baker. The LORD says, "Escape will fail the swift…" The swift are named right there in verse 14, next to the strong and the mighty.

Weapons are a smart guess, friend, but verse 14 doesn't say that. The LORD says, "Escape will fail the swift…" Then He goes on to say the strong will not prevail by his strength and the mighty will not save his life.
Horses do come up in the next verse, with the horseman (Amos 2:15). But for the swift in verse 14, the LORD says, "Escape will fail the swift…" Their getting away is what fails.
Not this time, baker. The LORD says, "…the horseman will not save his life." The horseman is named right there in verse 15, along with the archer and the fleet of foot.

Right, baker. The LORD says, "…the horseman will not save his life." He's listed in verse 15 along with the archer and the fleet of foot. So even the fastest rider in the bunch doesn't get away. The LORD also says that on that day even the bravest of mighty men will flee naked (Amos 2:16).
That's it, baker. The LORD says, "Even the bravest of mighty men will flee naked on that day…" Bravest is the word He uses, and even they flee.
Caves are a fine guess, but the verse doesn't say that. The LORD says, "Even the bravest of mighty men will flee naked on that day…" The verse says they flee, and it says naked, friend.

That's the opposite, friend. The LORD says the archer "…will not stand his ground…" (Amos 2:15), and then in verse 16 the bravest of mighty men "…will flee naked on that day…" Standing their ground is not what the bravest of mighty men do there.
